rewritten_text:
"Is that everything? Little enough, that! Plenty have incurred the Republic's displeasure and must peer through the little window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. Englishman. Which one is he?"

"I am. Necessarily, since I am the last."

Jarvis Lorry has answered every earlier question. Jarvis Lorry has stepped down and stands with one hand upon the carriage door, responding to the assembled officials. At their leisure they circle the coach and climb onto the box to inspect the small quantity of luggage upon its roof. The country people lingering nearby crowd closer to the doors, staring inside with eager eyes. A mother carrying a little child stretches out its short arm so that it may touch the wife of an aristocrat sent to the Guillotine.

"Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, countersigned."

"May one leave, citizen?"

"One may leave. Drive on, postilions! A pleasant journey!"

"My respects, citizens.—And the first peril behind us!"

Once more Jarvis Lorry speaks, clasping his hands and lifting his eyes. Inside the carriage there is fear, there are tears, there is the unconscious traveller's laboured breathing.

"Aren't we moving too slowly? Can't they be persuaded to hurry?" Lucie asks, clutching the old man.

"It would look like an escape, my dear. I dare not press them too hard; they would grow suspicious."

"Look behind us! Look and see whether anyone follows!"

"The road is empty, dearest. No one pursues us yet."

Groups of two or three houses slip past, isolated farms, decaying buildings, dye-works, tanneries, and similar places; then open fields and avenues of bare trees. Beneath us lies hard, uneven paving, with deep, soft mud along both sides. Sometimes we turn into the bordering mud to escape the stones that jolt and rattle us; sometimes we lodge in its ruts and mire. Then our impatience becomes such agony that, frantic with haste and terror, we long to climb out and run, to hide, to do anything rather than remain still.

Out of the open country and back among crumbling buildings, lonely farms, dye-works, tanneries, cottages in little clusters, and avenues of leafless trees. Have the men tricked us and returned by another route? Are we seeing the same place again? Heaven be thanked, no. A village. Look behind us, look for pursuit! Quiet—the posting-house.

Without haste our four horses are unharnessed. Without haste the horseless coach waits in the narrow street, looking as though it will never move again. Without haste the fresh horses materialize one at a time. Their new riders follow, sucking and braiding their whip lashes. Without haste the former postilions count their payment, add it wrongly, and reach unsatisfactory totals.

Yet he had tyrannized over nobody, confined nobody in prison. Far from enforcing harsh demands for what was owed him, he had freely surrendered his claims, ventured into an unfriendly world, established an independent place within it, and supported himself by his own labour. Monsieur Gabelle had managed the impoverished, indebted estate under written orders to spare its people and distribute whatever little remained available: winter fuel the powerful creditors would permit them, summer produce that could escape those same grasping hands. Undoubtedly Gabelle had pleaded these instructions and offered them as evidence for his own protection, so the truth must now emerge.

This encouraged the desperate intention Charles Darnay was beginning to form: he would travel to Paris.

Yes. Like the sailor of the ancient tale, wind and current had carried him within the power of the Loadstone Rock. It drew him irresistibly, and he must approach. Every thought that presented itself swept him faster and more steadily towards that dreadful attraction. Beneath his thoughts had lain the uneasiness that wicked purposes were being pursued by wicked agents in his unhappy homeland, while he, who could not help knowing himself better than they, remained absent instead of trying to restrain bloodshed and uphold mercy and humanity. Half smothered, half accusing him, that discomfort had brought him to a sharp comparison with the courageous old gentleman whose sense of duty was so powerful. Immediately after this comparison, unfavourable to himself, had come Monseigneur's sneers, which wounded him deeply, and Stryver's, especially coarse and irritating for reasons long established. Then came Gabelle's letter: an innocent captive facing death, appealing to his justice, his honour, and his reputation.

He had decided. Paris was where he must go.

Yes. The Loadstone Rock pulled him onward, and onward he must sail until he struck it. He was unaware of any rock and perceived almost no peril. The intention behind his former actions, unfinished though they remained, cast them in a light he believed France would gratefully recognize once he appeared to explain them. Then there rose before him that splendid dream of doing good which so often becomes the hopeful mirage of generous minds. Within the illusion he even imagined himself exerting some influence to direct the raging Revolution, now rushing so fearfully beyond restraint.

The great, ringing voice fell silent. It seemed almost beyond any physical instrument, for we could not connect such a sound with pipes or keys. The girl turned to help her elderly companion and finally saw us.

He was her father, and she had guided his blind steps since childhood. They were Germans from Saxony who had moved here only a few years earlier and made friends among the nearby villagers. Around the time the plague began, a young German student joined them. Their story was easy to understand. He was a nobleman who loved the poor musician's beautiful daughter. When they fled persecution by his friends, he followed. But soon death arrived with its sharp scythe, cutting down the tall flowers along with the grass and making everyone equal. The young man was an early victim. The girl kept herself alive for her father's sake. His blindness allowed her to maintain a misunderstanding that had first arisen by accident. Now they were the land's only survivors, yet he knew nothing of what had happened. When he listened to his daughter play, he did not realize that, apart from himself, her only audience was the silent mountains, the unfeeling lake, and the trees, which could not hear.

On the very day we reached them, she had developed signs of the illness. She was horrified by the thought of leaving her old, blind father alone in an empty world. Yet she could not bring herself to tell him the truth. Her desperate fear gave her strength to make extraordinary efforts. At the usual hour for evening prayer, she led him into the chapel. Though trembling and crying for him, she played the hymn celebrating the creation of the beautiful earth without a wrong note or a mistake in rhythm. That same earth would soon be her grave.

To her, we seemed like visitors from heaven. The moment help appeared, the courage and self-control she had struggled to maintain gave way. She screamed, rushed toward us, and clasped Adrian's knees. 'Oh, save my father!' were the only words she could manage. Then sobs and frantic cries released all the sorrow she had held back.

Poor girl! She and her father now rest side by side beneath the tall walnut tree where her lover lies. As she was dying, she pointed it out to us. Her father finally understood that she was in danger. Unable to see the changes in her beloved face, he held tightly to her hand until death made it cold and stiff. Even then he neither moved nor spoke. Twelve hours later, merciful death took him into endless rest. They lie beneath the grass, the tree serving as their memorial. I remember that sacred place clearly, enclosed by the rocky Jura and the distant, immense Alps. The spire of their church still rises among the surrounding trees. Her hand is cold now, but I imagine the heavenly music they loved still floating through the air, comforting their gentle ghosts.
